demographics.trauma_type: Accidentally caused serious injury to another

vignette:
At 22, he is only a few years into working as an HVAC technician, and before the accident he thinks of himself as steady with his hands, the kind of person who learns by doing. He likes the rhythm of the job: loading tools into the van before sunrise, climbing ladders, opening up metal units that hum and rattle on rooftops, figuring out what is wrong and fixing it. He is the oldest son in a Latin American family that depends on everyone pulling their weight, and he takes pride in bringing home a paycheck. He is single, living with relatives, joking easily at work, and trying to build a future one service call at a time.

The event happens on an ordinary weekday at a small commercial building. He is working with another technician who is older and more experienced. They are rushing because the client wants the cooling back on before the afternoon heat. He remembers being tired, wanting to prove he can keep up, and feeling embarrassed about asking the same safety question twice. He is handling a piece of equipment while the other man is positioned awkwardly near the unit. In a moment he replays over and over, he makes a decision too quickly. He activates or shifts the equipment before the other technician is fully clear. There is a sudden movement, a shout, then a sickening sound he still cannot describe without going quiet. The other man is badly injured.

What stays with him most is not just the image of the injury, but the split second after, when everything seems to go silent inside him. Then he is moving fast, yelling for help, calling emergency services, pressing his hands where someone tells him to press, staring at blood on his gloves. He rides the rest of that day in a fog. At the hospital and afterward, people tell him it was an accident, that no one thinks he meant to hurt anyone. He nods, but inside he begins saying something harsher: You did this. You should have checked again. You should have known.

In the weeks afterward, he tells himself he needs to be strong and keep working. Instead, his body starts reacting before his mind can catch up. When his alarm goes off before dawn, his chest tightens. On job sites, the sound of metal clanging or a motor suddenly kicking on makes him jerk and feel heat rush through him. He becomes painfully careful, checking every switch and lockout repeatedly, then checking again because he no longer trusts his own eyes. Simple tasks that used to feel automatic now take too long. He notices coworkers watching him, and their glances feel accusing even when they say nothing.

At night, the accident returns in fragments. Sometimes he sees the exact moment before it happened and wakes up drenched in sweat, his heart pounding so hard he sits on the edge of the bed and waits for the room to come back into focus. Other times he dreams that he injures someone else—his younger cousin, a stranger, anyone standing too close. He starts sleeping later and later because he dreads what he will see when he closes his eyes. In the morning he is exhausted and irritable, and his family experiences him as distant. He eats quickly, answers in one-word replies, and spends more time alone in his room with headphones on, though music does little to quiet his thoughts.

He avoids the injured coworker’s name. If someone from work brings up the accident, he leaves the room or pretends he has to answer a call. He stops driving past the building where it happened, even when it would save time. He turns down certain assignments and tells his supervisor he prefers maintenance calls over installations, though he cannot fully explain why. When he does have to work around similar equipment, he feels as if he is outside himself, hands moving but mind fixed on disaster. He imagines the worst outcome before every task. He watches where everyone is standing, where their fingers are, where a foot might slip, who might get crushed because of one mistake.

His guilt spreads beyond the accident. He starts believing he is dangerous, that maybe something is wrong with him, that if he gets close to people he will eventually hurt them too. He pulls back from friends who invite him out after work. He ignores texts from a woman he had been seeing casually because he cannot tolerate being asked, “What’s wrong?” His family encourages him to pray, rest, and let time do its job, but time seems only to deepen the groove the memory has cut into him. He becomes jumpy, ashamed of how easily he startles, ashamed of crying once in his van after hearing a compressor kick on.

Now, months later, he still shows up to work because not working feels impossible financially and humiliating personally. From the outside he looks functional: tool belt on, uniform clean, polite with customers. Inside, each day is organized around preventing another catastrophe. He scans constantly, sleeps poorly, and carries a private conviction that one careless second revealed his true nature. Even in safer moments, he cannot hold onto the idea that he is a good man who made a mistake. The accident remains present tense for him, as if some part of him is still standing beside that unit, waiting to undo what cannot be undone.
